extracted.intended_audience: novelists, literary observers and anyone curious about patterns in Booker Prize winners
extracted.subtask_description: An evidence-based, journalistic analysis of recurring features in past Booker Prize winners intended to suggest what kinds of novels and author profiles have tended to succeed. Summarises common book attributes, author demographics, timing/publisher patterns, stylistic and thematic tendencies, and notable anti-patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility / publication rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The Booker prize aims to spotlight “the finest in fiction”. Historically: a fine work of long-form fiction published in English within Britain over the preceding calendar year. In 2005 an international prize for translated books was introduced; in 2014 the main English-language prize was changed to include books written by authors from anywhere in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entries must be long-form fiction published in English within the relevant submission window; note the 2005 and 2014 changes broadening the prize's scope (translations and then authors of any nationality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Book length / physical heft
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'average book' winner is described as “A 408-page hardback of 581 grams”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heft appears to matter: very short works can be disadvantaged (example: Claire Keegan’s Small Things Like These at 116 pages/238g is said to 'lack heft' and this likely counts against it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing (month)
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners are often 'published in the May before the awards ceremony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing in the May ahead of the ceremony appears to be a common pattern among winners and may affect visibility/consideration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher profile
rubrics_metrics.description: The average winner was 'published by Bloomsbury'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Certain major literary publishers (Bloomsbury as cited) recurrently publish winners — publisher reputation/distribution may influence a book’s profile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred genre: historical fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: The average Booker-winning book 'is a work of historical fiction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical fiction is frequently represented among winners; by contrast, some genres (see anti-patterns) have 'traditionally failed to snag success.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Setting and timeframe
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners tend to be 'set in and around London' and, for the sample examined, 'some time during the 1980s.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: London features much more frequently than other cities (four times more often in the recent roster); specific period settings (e.g., 1980s) recur in winners' narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recurring themes
rubrics_metrics.description: Common thematic concerns include 'time and memory, love and loss, and family dynamics' and 'Colonialism and its after effects are major topics of interest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Books engaging with memory, family relationships and postcolonial issues (and political themes/satire) have frequently been selected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protagonist characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical protagonists are 'introspective', 'one with a career in the creative industries', and 'something of a social outcast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character types that are reflective, artistically involved and socially marginalised recur in winning novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative tense, perspective and viewpoint multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Winners are 'narrated in the past tense from either a first- or third-person perspective' and 'incorporates multiple viewpoints, many of them unexpected: think the recently deceased, or a herd of grazing cattle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past-tense narration and inventive or multiple perspectives (including unconventional narrators) are common formal features among winners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stylistic tendencies: sparse punctuation and political satire
rubrics_metrics.description: The average Booker book 'is sparse on punctuation, and heavy on political satire.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Economical punctuation and a satirical political edge are identified as stylistic tendencies in winners' prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cover aesthetics (visual cues)
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical winning book 'has a nice mid-blue front cover.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover colour/design recurs as a superficial but noted pattern; mid-blue covers appeared often among winners in the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author demographics and career stage
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'average author' is described as 'White, British, male, and aged 51 years and 6 months' with 'an established career... writing output of six books and one previous Booker shortlisting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically winners have tended to be established, middle-aged white British men with several prior books; despite efforts towards inclusivity this demographic pattern persists in the sample.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author multi-disciplinary experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Winning authors 'like to dabble in other mediums too, particularly poetry and screenwriting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors with a track record across literary forms (poetry, screenwriting) appear commonly among winners, suggesting breadth of literary practice matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior recognition (shortlisting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Having been 'previously shortlisted' is highlighted as a positive signal (NoViolet Bulawayo is noted as the only 2022 shortlisted author with a previous shortlisting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior Booker shortlisting (or similar recognition) correlates with stronger odds of winning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unfavoured features / genre taboos
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain features are cited as historically unsuccessful: 'trequel has never won', 'a novel with an exclamation mark in its title' has not won, and 'crime and black comedy... have traditionally failed to snag success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some formats/genres/titling conventions have little track record of success at the Booker and may reduce chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpredictability and role of luck
rubrics_metrics.description: The prize is described as unpredictable — likened to 'a chicken raffle' — implying luck plays a significant part in selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even with pattern-analysis, selection is partly contingent and unpredictable; statistical patterns narrow odds but do not determine outcomes.
